Status: accepted

Amends decision 11 and [ADR 4](/docs/decisions/adr-0004-management-api/).

## Context

[ADR 4](/docs/decisions/adr-0004-management-api/) put the management API behind an explicit
`api.enabled`, and decision 11 states the rule: the API is node-local, off by
default, and a node it has not claimed is in no cluster. The off-by-default half
was argued on one sentence, under *Alternatives considered*:

> **An always-on API with no way to switch it off.** Fewer states, one less key,
> and a fleet where `cctl` always works. Rejected because a privileged daemon
> listening on every machine is a reasonable thing to veto, and because a node
> that has been running happily for a year should not acquire a new listening
> port by being upgraded.

That reasoning is about a node **in service**. It says nothing about a node that
has just been installed and has never been told what it is — and that is the node
this record is about.

### The state the default produces

A machine installed from the published ISO with no cloud-init seed reaches a
state that is coherent, supported, and unusable:

- `corium-bootstrap` runs, finds no configuration, logs `no corium configuration
  found, leaving node unconfigured`, and writes no marker.
- `corium-apid` starts, `claimFromConfiguration` gets `source.ErrNotFound`, and
  the daemon exits 78. Nothing listens on 7443.
- No account exists. Corium creates no default user (decision 7 leaves accounts
  to cloud-init), and `PermitRootLogin` is `no`.
- The console prints `This node is not part of a cluster` above a login prompt
  nobody can answer.

The machine is healthy, reachable by ping, and there is no way in. Recovering it
means physical access: a `CIDATA` stick and a reboot, or a live system and a
write into `/var/lib/cloud/seed/nocloud` with the right SELinux label.

The project's own answer to this is `deploy/appliance/`, which bakes
`api.enabled: true` into `/usr/share/corium/config.yaml`. That answer works and
is documented, and it is a derived image nobody publishes. The recipe exists
because the published ISO cannot do the thing the recipe does — which is the
definition of a default in the wrong place.

### What the ISO makes different

ADR 4 was written when every route onto a node carried configuration with it:
cloud-init on a hypervisor, a metadata service on a cloud, a seed written by hand
in a rescue system. In all three, "no configuration" means somebody made a
mistake. The installer ISO broke that assumption. It is the one artefact that
installs a complete, running node while carrying nothing about what the node is —
that is what *unattended* means — and it is the artefact bare metal is supposed
to use.

So the question ADR 4 answered is not the question the ISO asks. ADR 4 asked
whether a node in service should grow a port. This asks whether a node that has
never been configured should be reachable at all.

## Decision

### 1. `api:` absent means the API runs

The `Mode()` default arm flips. An absent `api:` block no longer resolves to
`disabled`; it resolves to a new mode, **`enrollable`**, in which the daemon
serves and the enrolment route is open, authenticated by the pairing code on the
console exactly as mode C is today.

`api.enabled: false` keeps its meaning and stays the way to have no daemon and
no port. It is now the only way, which is the whole substance of this change.

### 2. `enrollable` serves, but does not hold the bootstrap

This is the distinction ADR 4 did not need and this record does. Today
`maintenance` means two things at once: serve the enrolment route, **and** hold
the node's bootstrap until an operator claims it. Flipping the default without
separating them would make every existing single-line configuration hold its
bootstrap forever, waiting for an operator who was never coming.

So they separate. `HoldsBootstrap()` stays exactly what it is — true only for
`maintenance`, which an operator still asks for by writing `api.enabled: true`
with no CA, as [`awaiting-config.yaml`](https://github.com/Corium-OS/Corium/blob/main/docs/examples/awaiting-config.yaml) does.
`enrollable` serves the port and lets the bootstrap proceed. A node with
`role: single` and no `api:` block behaves on first boot exactly as it does
today, and additionally answers on 7443 while it is getting there.

### 3. Enrolment closes when the node bootstraps

ADR 4's central invariant is that a node is never simultaneously valuable and
unclaimed:

> **Letting an unenrolled node join the cluster and enrol later.** [...] it costs
> a node that is simultaneously valuable and unclaimed — running workloads,
> holding cluster credentials, and waiting to obey whoever reaches an
> unauthenticated port first. The pairing code was invented to defend that state.
> Deleting the state is better than defending it.

That invariant survives this record unchanged, and it is what bounds the change.
The enrolment route is served **only while `/var/lib/corium/bootstrapped` is
absent**. A node that has bootstrapped — that holds cluster credentials and may
be running workloads — refuses to be claimed, whatever its configuration says.
Taking such a node over still requires `cctl reset`, as it does today.

This is stricter than the current code, which gates enrolment on
`store.Enrolled()` alone. A node that bootstrapped and was later given
`api.enabled: true` by hand can be claimed today; it cannot after this record.
That is a deliberate tightening, and it is the price of the default being on.

### 4. The daemon runs where it can do something

The three rules above leave one state with no purpose: a node that bootstrapped
from its own configuration, was never claimed, and names no operator CA. Its
enrolment route is closed by rule 3 and it has no CA to authenticate anyone
with, so it would listen on 7443 for the rest of its life and refuse every
request. That is attack surface with no capability attached, which is the thing
ADR 4's veto was actually about.

So `corium-apid` serves when either half is true, and exits 78 otherwise:

- **the node is still enrollable** — not bootstrapped, and not `api.enabled:
  false`; or
- **the node has an owner** — it has adopted an operator CA, by enrolment or from
  `api.operatorCA`.

Every node is therefore either claimable or already answerable, and no node
carries a port that can do nothing. "On by default" is a statement about what an
operator has to write, not a promise that a socket exists on every machine in
every state.

### 5. The pairing code stays the default, and `insecure` stays opt-in

Nothing about authentication changes. A node with no configuration mints a
pairing code, prints it on the console, and requires it. `api.insecure: true`
still drops the code for a bench or a provisioning network, still logs a warning,
and is still recorded as `ClaimedOpenly` in the claim method `cctl status`
reports.

This is the line between this record and `deploy/appliance/`. The appliance sets
`insecure: true`, and its README is blunt about what that costs: *the first
client to reach port 7443 owns the machine for the rest of its life*. This record
makes the **port** default, not the **openness**. An attacker on the network
still cannot claim a node they cannot see the console of.

### 6. A document that names no role still needs an explicit `api:`

`role` may be omitted only when the API is on — a rule that exists so a
configuration with a typo in `role:` is refused at validation rather than
producing a node that waits forever. Flipping the default would silently retire
it.

It does not, because the two cases are different in kind. Validation runs on a
document; the ISO case has no document at all. A document that names no role and
no `api:` block is still refused, with the error it gives today. Writing a
configuration that says nothing is a mistake. Shipping no configuration is a
choice, and it is the choice this record serves.

## Consequences

**A node installed from the ISO is enrollable.** It prints a pairing code on its
console and waits, indefinitely, in no cluster and having changed nothing about
itself. `cctl enroll <address> --code <code> --config node.yaml` makes it a node.
That is the point of the record.

**Nodes in service acquire a listening port on upgrade — some of them.** This is
the cost ADR 4 declined to pay, and it is now paid in part. A node that was
claimed, or that names an operator CA, already had the daemon. A node that
bootstrapped from its own configuration and was never claimed does not gain one,
because rule 4 exits it. What gains a port is the window between boot and
bootstrap on every node: roughly a minute, with a pairing code that closes
permanently when k0s comes up.

That window is new and it is real. It is bounded by the console requirement: an
attacker who can reach 7443 during that minute still needs the code, and the code
is on a channel they do not have.

**`deploy/appliance/` loses most of its reason to exist.** What remains of it is
`insecure: true` and `awaitConfig: true` — the zero-console posture — which this
record deliberately does not make default. The recipe stays; its README gains a
line saying the port is now default and only the openness is not.

**One more state to hold in your head.** `Mode()` grows a fourth value, and the
answer to "is the API on?" becomes two questions rather than one. That is the
honest cost of rule 4, and the alternative was a dead socket on every node.

**Reverting is a configuration change, not a rollback.** A fleet that wants the
old posture writes `api.enabled: false`. There is no image-level switch, and
adding one would be a second authority over the same question.

## Alternatives considered

**Leave the default off and publish the appliance image.** The smallest change:
no ADR, no code, one more artefact in the release. Rejected because it makes the
answer to "how do I install on bare metal" depend on which of two images you
happened to pull, and because the appliance's posture is `insecure: true`, which
is not a thing to publish as the bare-metal path.

**On by default only while the node is unbootstrapped.** Considered first, and it
is very nearly rule 4 arrived at from the other side. It differs on a node that
was claimed and then bootstrapped: that node has an owner and must keep
answering, so the rule has to mention ownership anyway. Stating both halves is
clearer than stating one and patching it.

**On by default, with enrolment staying open until the node is claimed rather
than until it bootstraps.** Strictly more useful: a node in service that nobody
owns could still be adopted. Rejected on ADR 4's invariant, which is the load-
bearing one in that record — it recreates precisely the node that is valuable and
unclaimed, and it does so by default rather than by an operator's choice.

**A timeout: listen for N minutes after boot, then stop.** Shrinks the exposure
window, and creates a state where a machine is neither configured nor reachable
and recovery is a physical visit again — which is the problem this record exists
to remove. The window is already bounded by bootstrap for a configured node, and
for an unconfigured one the whole point is that it waits.

**Make `insecure` the default too, matching the appliance.** It would make bare
metal genuinely zero-touch, which is the one thing the pairing code costs. It is
the model ADR 4 argued against at length and offered as an opt-in with the
argument left standing. Nothing here weakens that argument; a default that hands
a machine to whoever reaches it first is not a default.
